summary.text: Correlation is a statistical relationship between two random variables, usually meaning how far a pair of quantities are linearly related.
The common Pearson coefficient divides the covariance by the product of the two standard deviations, which gives a value between -1 and +1.
Correlation does not imply causation, and a correlation of 0 does not mean the variables are independent.

facts.label: Perfect line
facts.value: +1 for a perfect rising line, -1 for a perfect falling line

facts.label: Near zero
facts.value: The closer to zero, the less of a relationship

facts.label: What Pearson detects
facts.value: Only linear dependencies between two variables

facts.label: Rank coefficients
facts.value: Spearman's and Kendall's check whether one tends to rise as the other rises

facts.label: Who developed it
facts.value: Karl Pearson, from a similar idea by Francis Galton

items.prompt: An electrical utility plans to produce less power on a mild day, because demand tracks the weather. What makes the correlation useful here?

options.label: It indicates a predictive relationship that can be used in practice
It proves that mild weather is the only cause of demand
It shows demand and weather are independent
It removes the need to measure demand

items.explain: Correlations are useful because they can point to a predictive relationship that can be exploited, as the utility does.

items.prompt: Sales of sunscreen and ice cream rise and fall together over the year. Can you conclude that one causes the other?

options.label: Yes, any strong correlation shows cause
Yes, but only if the correlation is exactly +1
Only if sales are measured in the same units
No, correlation alone is not enough to infer cause

items.explain: The presence of a correlation is not sufficient to infer a causal relationship.

items.prompt: X is spread evenly on both sides of zero, and Y = X². What is true of X and Y?

options.label: They are independent, since the correlation is zero
Y depends fully on X, yet their correlation is zero
Their correlation must be +1, since Y follows X
Their correlation must be -1, since Y is a square

items.explain: Y is completely determined by X, but the relationship is not a straight line, so the correlation is zero and they are uncorrelated.

items.prompt: Someone reports a correlation coefficient of 1.4 between two measures. What should you conclude?

options.label: The relationship is stronger than a perfect line
The measures are independent
Something is wrong, since it must lie from -1 to +1
It shows a perfect falling relationship

items.explain: The absolute value of Pearson's coefficient cannot exceed 1, so the value ranges only from -1 to +1.

items.prompt: Two variables are independent of each other. What can you say about their Pearson correlation coefficient?

options.label: It is exactly 1
It is exactly -1
Somewhere between 0 and 1
It is 0

items.explain: Independent variables are uncorrelated, so the coefficient is 0. The reverse does not hold: a coefficient of 0 does not guarantee independence.

items.prompt: Each time x goes up, y goes up too, but the points bend along a curve rather than a straight line. Which kind of measure reads this as a perfect relationship?

options.label: Pearson's coefficient, which needs a straight line
Every coefficient gives the same value
No coefficient, as the points are off a line
A rank coefficient such as Spearman's

items.explain: Rank coefficients check whether one variable tends to rise as the other rises, so they can reach 1 here, while Pearson's value falls short because the points are not on a straight line.

paragraphs.heading: What correlation means
paragraphs.text: Correlation is a kind of statistical relationship between two random variables, or between two sets of paired data. It usually means how closely the two quantities follow a straight-line relationship. Any relationship at all between variables, linear or not, is called an association: the degree to which the ups and downs of one can be explained by the other.

paragraphs.heading: Useful, but not proof of cause
paragraphs.text: Correlations matter because they can point to a relationship you can use to predict. A power company, for instance, may generate less electricity on a mild day, based on the link between weather and demand. In that case there really is a cause, since extreme weather makes people use more power for heating or cooling. But a correlation alone is not enough to show a cause, a point usually put as "correlation does not imply causation".

paragraphs.heading: Pearson's coefficient
paragraphs.text: The most common measure is the Pearson correlation coefficient, which Karl Pearson built from a similar idea by Francis Galton. You get it by dividing the covariance by the product of the two variables' standard deviations. Its value always lies between −1 and +1. It is +1 for a perfect rising straight-line relationship and −1 for a perfect falling one. The nearer it is to zero, the weaker the relationship; the nearer to −1 or 1, the stronger.

paragraphs.heading: Zero does not mean unrelated
paragraphs.text: If two variables are independent, their Pearson coefficient is 0. The reverse is not guaranteed, because the coefficient only picks up linear links. Take a variable X spread symmetrically around zero, and let Y = X². Y is completely fixed by X, yet their correlation is zero. One special case is different: when X and Y are jointly normal, being uncorrelated is the same as being independent.

paragraphs.heading: Rank correlation
paragraphs.text: Rank correlation coefficients, such as Spearman's and Kendall's (τ), ask whether one variable tends to rise as the other rises, without needing the rise to follow a straight line. If one falls as the other rises, they come out negative. Take a set of pairs where y goes up every time x goes up. Spearman's and Kendall's coefficients are both 1, but Pearson's is only 0.7544, because the points sit far from a straight line. Rank coefficients are best seen as measuring a different kind of association, not as stand-ins for Pearson's.

paragraphs.heading: Two practical notes
paragraphs.text: When the measured values carry measurement error, the realistic range of the coefficient is narrower than −1 to +1. And when a linear model has just one independent variable, R squared (the coefficient of determination) equals the square of Pearson's coefficient.
